Information and transfer

Retained judgment

Within the information experiment, prediction error follows from the signals actually processed before a later unaided judgment.

To follow what a junior preparer retains from a worked return, we represent the needed foundation and later target judgment by independent symmetric signs BBB and TTT. Observations S=BηS=B\etaS=Bη and Y=BTϵY=BT\epsilonY=BTϵ contain independent noise with means rBr_BrB​ and rAr_ArA​, and averaging over the unknown foundation gives Pr⁡(Y=y∣T=t)=1/2\Pr(Y=y\mid T=t)=1/2Pr(Y=y∣T=t)=1/2, so the explanation alone leaves the target’s prior unchanged while the joint likelihood retains the shared foundation.

Bayes’ rule applied to that likelihood gives posterior mean rBrASYr_Br_A SYrB​rA​SY, and because T2=1T^2=1T2=1, its conditional variance is 1−rB2rA21-r_B^2r_A^21−rB2​rA2​. Independent receipt of the foundational observation with probability ppp averages that risk with the prior risk of one, yielding expected risk 1−prB2rA21-pr_B^2r_A^21−prB2​rA2​, which connects receipt of the record pair to the expected error of later judgment (fig. 2).

For several uncertain principles, a Gaussian prior provides the same logic through covariance overlap, since an exercise helps a later target to the extent that their uncertain components move together. Proposition A.1 and its corollary prove these statements and identify equality of processed information as the condition under which a customer file preserves the learning occasion.

Binary posterior

Summing the conditional probabilities over the two foundation values cancels terms linear in the foundation and retains the product of signal reliabilities, giving the likelihood below. Changing one observed sign reverses the direction of the posterior mean while preserving its magnitude, so the favored target changes while uncertainty remains the same. Across all four signal pairs, squaring that mean gives the same variance reduction, allowing observed answers to differ while the information quality associated with the experiment remains fixed.

Announced machine improvements

With both paths interior mixed, frontier output depends only on the machine method, so identical pre-adoption methods give identical pre-adoption frontiers and wages. Lower subsequent machine requirements raise the scalar frontier field, while machine productivity elasticity at least as large as human productivity elasticity keeps the improved equal-cost wage weakly decreasing along that faster frontier, giving the future wage ordering that the positive career-value kernel transmits to current study.

Resource clock

Multiplying A˙=BR(t)A−ϕ/[q(t)aM(A)]\dot A=B_R(t)A^{-\phi}/[q(t)a_M(A)]A˙=BR​(t)A−ϕ/[q(t)aM​(A)] by AϕaM(A)A^\phi a_M(A)AϕaM​(A) and integrating gives equality between required cumulative research effort and cumulative purchasing power. When total effort to reach arbitrarily large frontiers is finite, the arrival date is finite if the resource clock reaches that value, while a resource clock whose limit remains smaller yields a bounded frontier.

Because the required-effort integral is strictly increasing in its upper frontier limit, its inverse converts accumulated research purchasing power into a unique frontier while that power stays below the integral’s limiting value. Through this representation, a production endpoint is located by the effort needed for further advances, and its calendar date follows the resources that the research economy supplies over time.

For frontier-indexed asymptotic resources, direct substitution gives drift proportional to ApM+βB−βq−ϕA^{p_M+\beta_B-\beta_q-\phi}ApM​+βB​−βq​−ϕ, so the same power integration places the finite-arrival threshold at pM+βB−βq>1+ϕp_M+\beta_B-\beta_q>1+\phipM​+βB​−βq​>1+ϕ. Households and learning

Gary S. Becker (1965). A Theory of the Allocation of Time. Economic Journal 75(299), 493–517. Household time and purchased inputs enter a common production account.

Kenneth J. Arrow (1962). The Economic Implications of Learning by Doing. Review of Economic Studies 29(3), 155–173. Current production supplies experience that can improve future performance.

Daron Acemoglu, Pascual Restrepo (2019). Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor. Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(2), 3–30. Labor demand depends on the tasks assigned to labor and capital.

Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu, Haosen Ge, Özge Kabakcı, Rei Mariman (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26), e2422633122. Tool design affected subsequent unaided performance in a mathematics field experiment.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey Raymond (2025). Generative AI at Work. Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), 889–942. Customer-support evidence connects assistance to experience-dependent gains and worker learning.

Skills and institutions

Gary S. Becker (1962). Investment in Human Capital: A Theoretical Analysis. Journal of Political Economy 70(5, Part 2), 9–49. Workers capture returns to portable general skills in competitive labor markets.

Yoram Ben-Porath (1970). The Production of Human Capital Over Time. Education, Income, and Human Capital, edited by W. Lee Hansen, NBER, 129–154. Human-capital investment is evaluated across the worker’s life cycle.

Luis Garicano (2000). Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production. Journal of Political Economy 108(5), 874–904. Specialized knowledge is organized around the problems people can solve.

Daron Acemoglu, Jörn-Steffen Pischke (1999). The Structure of Wages and Investment in General Training. Journal of Political Economy 107(3), 539–572. Wage compression changes employers’ incentives to finance general training.

Uwe Dulleck, Rudolf Kerschbamer (2006). On Doctors, Mechanics, and Computer Specialists: The Economics of Credence Goods. Journal of Economic Literature 44(1), 5–42. Expert-service markets combine diagnosis with customers’ difficulty evaluating treatment.

Research and growth

Benjamin F. Jones (2009). The Burden of Knowledge and the “Death of the Renaissance Man”: Is Innovation Getting Harder?. Review of Economic Studies 76(1), 283–317. Accumulating knowledge connects educational burden, specialization, and teamwork.

Anton Korinek, Donghyun Suh (2024). Scenarios for the Transition to AGI. NBER Working Paper 32255. Wage paths depend on how automation proceeds alongside capital accumulation.

Paul M. Romer (1990). Endogenous Technological Change. Journal of Political Economy 98(5, Part 2), S71–S102. Nonrival ideas connect research investment to benefits beyond one producer.

Nicholas Bloom, Charles I. Jones, John Van Reenen, Michael Webb (2020). Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?. American Economic Review 110(4), 1104–1144. Measured research productivity declines across several industries, products, and firms.

Charles I. Jones, Christopher Tonetti (2026). Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion. Working paper, May 2026, version 0.5. Complementary tasks limit gains from partial automation while goods and ideas become automated.

Philippe Aghion, Benjamin F. Jones, Charles I. Jones (2019). Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth. The Economics of Artificial Intelligence: An Agenda, University of Chicago Press. Automating goods and ideas links AI to growth and the allocation of income.
